thread.title: Dell's Decision To Return To Public Trading - Dell Technologies Inc. (NYSE:DELL)

author: Sam Warren
title: Dell's Decision To Return To Public Trading - Dell Technologies Inc. (NYSE:DELL)
text:
After spending a half-decade as a private company, Dell Technologies ( DELL ) has returned to the New York Stock Exchange as of December 28 th . Shares were trading at $45.13 on the 28 th , up 3% since its initial IPO price of $31.30.
Recently, Dell surpassed HP as the world’s largest server maker in terms of revenue. This, among other reasons, poised the PC producer to make a return to the public markets. Dell had considered an IPO, in order to halt criticism by investors of DVMT such as Carl Icahn and Elliott Management, but ended up with a deal. For information regarding the public equity market move, Miriam Gottfried explores the $24 billion cash-and-equity deal that leaves DVMT retired and unlisted here .
What’s Different: Revamped for Cloud Computing Michael Dell took his company private back in 2013 and returned it to the public markets with a new model. The company built up value, especially through its VMware systems and modernized around cloud technology - a market expected to be worth $300 billion by 2021.
What Dell and his management team realized was that the world was changing around him. Rather than stay stagnant, the move to become private helped his corporation adapt to the world of cloud computing and the role that data-powered software has come to play. In the evolving PC market, Dell has found success in infrastructure, including x86 servers, storage, and server virtualization.
The keys to keeping DELL in the green can be found in the company’s four core business segments: PCs, Servers, Storage, and VMware.
Financials
(Source: July Investor Presentation )
PCs
Dell is the world’s third-largest PC producer, behind competitors HP Inc. ( HPQ ) and Lenovo ( OTCPK:LNVGY ). Although the PC market has been in a decline throughout the last decade, thanks to the success of Apple ( AAPL ) computers, the market has been stabilizing over the past two years. Dell is projecting global PC revenue to compound annually by about 2% through 2021.
This is a modest but positive sign for Dell, as the PC maker represents an 18.1% PC unit share (calendar Q2), up from 17% in Q2 2017.
(Source: July Investor Presentation)
In an investor meeting in July, management expressed to investors how the PC market has been consolidating in the last 5 years. The big three (Dell, HP, and Lenovo) have surpassed all other PC producers in PC unit share. Other key players have either left the market or are planning exits from their PC businesses. This leaves more margins for the Big 3.
(Source: July Investor Presentation)
Servers
Dell has passed HP as the world’s largest service maker in terms of revenue. It boasts an 18.8% server share, up 17.7% YOY. The company’s server revenue rose 20% in fiscal 2018 to $12.8 billion. This is an industry with a cloudy future - ironically enough, due to the cloud infrastructure adoption many businesses are pursuing. In fact, HP decided back in 2017 to stop selling hyperscale servers that it used to sell to cloud providers. The margins in this market are slim, and hardware is not a big profit generator. Dell has exposure to the cloud computing industry, and this exposure is likely to offset any negative pushback to its server businesses.
(Source: July Investor Presentation)
Storage
This business segment is faltering to competitors such as NetApp ( NTAP ) and Pure Storage ( PSTG ). Dell’s revenue for storage markets fell 11% to $4.2 billion. Dell has plans to revitalize this segment of its business, but with cloud storage adoption growing so pervasively, it is likely that the company will need to pick it up in other sectors to make up for lost profits. One of these sectors is the server virtualization business.
VMware
VMware has seen positive growth over the last fiscal year. In Quarter 1 of fiscal year 2018, Dell reported $1.8 billion in VMware revenue. Dell is projecting $2.0 billion in revenue for Quarter 1 of 2019, representing growth of 12%. By the end of fiscal 2019, this segment is expected to grow 8% to $8.8 billion, while net income is projected to be $2.5 billion (+19%).
The focal point of VMware - vSphere - has taken a hit over the past couple of years due to stiff competition, but Dell has seen growth for platforms such as vSAN, NSX, and Workspace ONE. The pressures and competition for vSphere will persist in 2019, but rising sales to cloud partners have helped VMware stay positive.
VMware has been active in cloud operations. Recently with the acquisition of Heptio, a Kubernetes company, and CloudHealth, Dell has positioned itself to handle multi-cloud operations.
Conclusion VMware expanded its cloud computing alliance with Amazon Web Services, the cloud partner of Amazon ( AMZN ), this past week. Moves such as this have JPMorgan advocating very strongly for the company as it moves into 2019. Characterized as a “formidable leader in IT client solutions,” JPMorgan rated the stock overweight , making it a value play even as the price rose in December 29 th trading. JPMorgan also issued a $60 price target, which implies a 34% growth rate for the share price.
If you are an investor in DELL, you have long been aware of the criticism cast on the company on account of its accrued debt. This is a reality, and the company will have to trade innovation for paying down this debt in order to bolster its credit rating. However, there is value in Dell on account of its emerging businesses, especially VMware. As Forbes writer John Furrier puts it, “If VMware is worth $65b and Dell owns 80% of VMware then that’s $52b in value right there. So, at the moment, the Dell Technologies valuation looks good at $33b.”
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions.
